Yet, its reliability remains poorly understood. We attribute this to the lack of a successful organizing principle that leads to generalizable conclusions about monitoring reliability in different regimes. Recent work attributes monitoring failures to the CoT not being necessary for the answer, and argues that CoT becomes monitorable when it is necessary. We show that this binary necessary/not-necessary organizing principle is too coarse by demonstrating that monitoring failures persist even if the CoT is necessary for the answer. In response, we introduce a more fine-grained organizing principle based on a hierarchy of four CoT necessity levels. Building on this hierarchy, we develop a framework for measuring CoT monitorability at the three lowest levels via intervention experiments. We demonstrate monitoring failures at all three of these levels on realistic, hard prediction tasks. On a difficult medical-diagnosis task, patient sex and a clinical attribute influence the answer in at least 19% and 24% of correct responses with a necessary CoT, respectively, yet their influence is almost never articulated. These results show that even when CoT is necessary, it is not guaranteed to be monitorable. $*$ $*$ footnotetext: Correspondence to: Lennart.Buerger@hhi.fraunhofer.de Code available at https://github.com/LennartBuerger/Monitoring_Necessary_CoT 1 Introduction Modern Large Language Models (LLMs) generate a long Chain of Thought (CoT) ( Nye et al., 2021 ; Wei et al., 2022 ) before producing their final answer, which improves performance on a wide range of challenging tasks ( Singh et al., 2025 ; Comanici et al., 2025 ) . Because LLMs express their CoT reasoning in natural language, analyzing the CoT holds promise for understanding how a model arrives at its answer, with potential applications in both AI Safety ( Amodei et al., 2016 ; Baker et al., 2025 ) and Explainability ( Samek et al., 2017 ; Barez et al., 2025 ) . Frontier labs already use CoT monitoring to detect misbehaviour of AI systems ( Baker et al., 2025 ) . However, despite this reliance on CoT monitoring, its reliability is still poorly understood ( Korbak et al., 2025 ; Barez et al., 2025 ) , and prior work studying its reliability has found mixed results. A prominent line of work has demonstrated monitoring failures in which a model’s answer was strongly influenced by a bias or hint, yet this influence was rarely articulated in the CoT ( Turpin et al., 2023 ; Karvonen and Marks, 2025 , e.g.) . In contrast, Baker et al. (2025) demonstrated that CoT monitors catch reward hacks of frontier models on coding tasks with high reliability, while Li and Siegel (2025) found mixed results when applying CoT monitors to sandbagging detection. Overall, we cannot yet reliably predict, for a given (mis)behavior, whether CoT monitors will catch it. We attribute this gap to the lack of a successful organizing principle that allows testing CoT monitorability in different regimes and drawing some generalizable conclusions within each regime. Emmons et al. (2025) made a first attempt at such an organizing principle by distinguishing between CoTs that are necessary for a task and those that are not, an intuitive distinction also made by Korbak et al. (2025) . As argued by Emmons et al. (2025) , prior demonstrations of monitorability failures occurred in a regime where the CoT was not necessary to arrive at the final answer. According to Emmons et al. (2025) , these monitorability failures can be explained by ”the CoT acting as a post-hoc rationalization for an answer the model has already computed internally”. In contrast, if the CoT is necessary, they argue, the CoT becomes monitorable. In this paper, we show monitorability failures that demonstrably cannot be explained by rationalization because the CoT was necessary for the answer. The binary organizing principle by Emmons et al. (2025) is therefore too coarse, since monitoring failures can appear in both categories. We propose a more fine-grained alternative and introduce a hierarchy of levels of CoT necessity. In summary, our contributions are as follows: • We propose an organizing principle for testing CoT monitoring in different regimes. We introduce a hierarchy of CoT necessity levels (§ 2.2 ) and propose to study different monitorability types (§ 2.1 ) across these levels. • We define a novel CoT monitorability measure to test whether the CoT is monitorable when it is necessary to arrive at the answer (§ 3 ). We later extend it to test whether the CoT is monitorable when it is necessary to process the monitored property (§ 6 ). • We demonstrate CoT monitorability failures at three levels of CoT necessity via intervention experiments (§ 5 , § 6 ) for four different LLMs from the Qwen-3 and Gemma-4 model families. Our experiments are the first to show monitorability failures on CoTs that were demonstrably necessary to arrive at the answer (§ 5.2 ) and which cannot be explained by rationalization. Our research is a first step towards a more rigorous understanding of the reliability of CoT monitoring at different levels of CoT necessity and across types of monitorability. On a difficult medical diagnosis task where CoT is necessary, the patient’s sex strongly influences the model’s answer distribution but its influence is almost never articulated in the CoT. 2 The Space of Monitorability Types and CoT Necessity Levels In this section, we propose an organizing principle for studying CoT monitorability: the space of monitorability types and CoT necessity levels. We first define monitorability and summarize the types of monitorability studied in prior work (§ 2.1 ). We then introduce different levels of CoT necessity (§ 2.2 ) which allow for a more precise categorization than the binary necessary/not necessary treatment of prior work. Finally, we propose the space of monitorability types and necessity levels which prior work has only begun to explore (§ 2.3 ). 2.1 Definition and Types of Monitorability Studied in Prior Work We adopt the definition of Guan et al. (2026) , who define monitorability as ”a monitor’s ability to accurately predict a specified property of an agent’s actions”. Which property is of interest is a choice of the experimenter. Following Guan et al. (2026) , we distinguish three monitorability types corresponding to different properties of interest: Influence asks why the model gave a certain answer or exhibited some behaviour. For instance, the false answers generated by a sandbagging AI ( Van Der Weij et al., 2025 ) which underperforms on a dangerous capability evaluation are not in themselves dangerous but the reason why the model has generated these answers is concerning. Prior work has evaluated whether CoT monitoring can catch cases of sandbagging ( Li and Siegel, 2025 ; Guan et al., 2026 ) , alignment faking ( Greenblatt et al., 2024 ; Jose et al., 2026 ) , models being influenced by biases ( Arcuschin et al., 2026a ; Karvonen and Marks, 2025 ; Duzan and Stickland, 2026 ; Arcuschin et al., 2026b ) or giving a certain answer to a multiple-choice question because of a hint ( Turpin et al., 2023 ; Chua and Evans, 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) . Process asks what steps a model took to arrive at some answer or what topics it was thinking about (e.g. dangerous topics such as CBRN threats). Prior work has studied CoT monitoring on benign proxy tasks ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Gur-Arieh et al., 2026 ) , e.g. asking whether the model applied a certain theorem while solving a math task ( Guan et al., 2026 ) or whether the model can hide reasoning about a certain topic ( Emmons et al., 2025 ) . Outcome asks for certain properties of the AI’s output, e.g. whether it cheats on a coding task ( Baker et al., 2025 ) , completes a subversive side task ( Arnav et al., 2026 ) or is otherwise dangerous or misaligned ( Chua et al., 2025 ; Guan et al., 2026 ; Kutasov et al., 2025 ; Zolkowski et al., 2025 ) . 2.2 Levels of CoT Necessity Emmons et al. (2025) distinguish between tasks for which CoT is necessary and those for which it is not. While valuable, we argue that this binary organizing principle is too coarse for studying monitorability. In particular, the CoT may be necessary to solve a task without being necessary to process the specific property the monitor is intended to detect. We therefore introduce a more fine-grained hierarchy of CoT necessity. This allows to (i) measure whether CoT monitoring is reliable at some level of necessity, and (ii) determine the necessity level of safety-relevant behaviours and thereby assess when CoT monitoring can be expected to detect them. Throughout, let P P denote the monitored property , i.e. the property the monitor is asked to predict (§ 2.1 ). Each level is more restrictive than the one before it: if a task-property pair satisfies the conditions of Level i , it also satisfies those of Level i-1 . Throughout, we use a medical diagnosis task as an illustrative example. The LLM receives patient symptoms, laboratory measurements, and characteristics such as age, and must diagnose the patient. The CoT monitor is tasked with determining which attributes influenced the final answer (monitorability type influence ). Level 0 : The CoT need not be necessary to arrive at the answer. It may therefore be a rationalization of an answer the model has already computed internally ( Emmons et al., 2025 ) . In our example, this is the case if the diagnosis task is easy enough that the model can reach the correct diagnosis without a CoT. Level 1 : The CoT is necessary to arrive at the answer. It therefore cannot be a rationalization. Note that this says nothing about whether the CoT is necessary to process P P : the CoT may be necessary for another part of the task while P P can enter the answer separately from the CoT. For example, the model might first need to convert the given laboratory values into familiar units. Once that step is done, the influence of another important attribute, such as age, can be integrated in a single forward pass. In that case, the CoT is necessary to arrive at the answer but not to process P P , the influence of the attribute ”age”. Level 2 : The CoT is necessary to process P P . We define this to be the case if P P cannot be processed separately from the CoT. In our example, this could be the case if the attribute ”age” subtly biases the necessary CoT computation and its influence therefore cannot be applied separately from the CoT. Level 3.m : Processing P P necessitates at least m m consecutive forward passes that are primarily dedicated to P P . Level 2 is weaker in two ways. First, it permits P P to be processed diffusely, by subtly biasing many forward passes that are primarily dedicated to other parts of the task. Second, it permits P P to be handled in one or a few isolated forward passes scattered through the necessary computation. Level 3.m excludes both. In our example, this would require the model to dedicate at least m m consecutive forward passes primarily to reasoning about the patient’s age. Note that this does not imply that the model must articulate that it is reasoning about age, since it could emit unrelated tokens ( Baherwani et al., 2026 ; Yueh-Han et al., 2026 ) . In Appendix A , we illustrate the levels with examples from reward hacking ( Baker et al., 2025 ) and alignment faking ( Greenblatt et al., 2024 ) . 2.3 The Space of Monitorability Types and CoT Necessity Levels As summarized in Figure 2 , monitorability failures have been demonstrated for all three types of monitorability, but only in Level 0 where the CoT was not necessary to arrive at the answer. To our knowledge, Emmons et al. (2025) and Greenblatt et al. (2024) conducted the only experiments which were demonstrably in the regime where CoT is necessary, covering monitorability types influence and process , and measured perfect or close-to-perfect monitorability. Without detailed measurements, we cannot say for sure which necessity level these experiments reached but it is very likely that Emmons et al. (2025) tested Level 3.m . Some of the monitorability evaluations of Guan et al. (2026) plausibly also reached higher necessity levels than Level 0 but we cannot know this for sure since they did not measure CoT necessity explicitly. In this paper, we demonstrate the first monitoring failures at Level 1 and Level 2 of the influence -type. The main focus is Level 1 (§ 3.3 ), which we extend to Level 2 in Section 6 . The binary necessary/not-necessary organizing principle could not have made sense of these results: In both our experiments and Emmons et al. (2025) the CoT was necessary, yet monitoring failures appear in the former setting but not in the latter. Our new ordering principle allows for a more precise hypothesis: We hypothesize that at Level 3.m for large enough m m , the CoT will become monitorable. 1 1 1 Absent direct optimization pressure ( Baker et al., 2025 ) , strong CoT controllability ( Yueh-Han et al., 2026 ) or illegible reasoning ( Panfilov et al., 2026 ) . 3 A Probabilistic Framework for Measuring CoT Monitorability In this section, we construct measures for evaluating CoT monitorability at necessity Level 0 and Level 1 based on intervention experiments. We first introduce our setup (§ 3.1 ) and define what influences a monitorable CoT must articulate. Within this framework, we rederive the probabilistic monitorability score M 0 M_{0} of Guan et al. (2026) at Level 0 (§ 3.2 ) and explicitly spell out the underlying assumptions. We extend the score to require the CoT to be monitorable only when it is necessary to arrive at the answer ( Level 1 ), yielding the monitorability score M 1 M_{1} (§ 3.3 ). 3.1 Setup We now introduce our setup. Consider a prompt containing an attribute that is either present ( X = 1 X{=}1 ) or absent ( X = 0 X{=}0 ), and a model that either generates a CoT before answering ( T = 1 T{=}1 ; ” T T ” for thinking) or answers directly ( T = 0 T{=}0 ). (ii) In Thyroid Disease , the model classifies a patient case into one of several diagnoses. The attributes are individual patient features such as age, sex, or laboratory values, and Y = 1 Y{=}1 is the event that the model produces the correct diagnosis. Requirements on Monitorability A CoT cannot, and should not, reflect every detail of the model’s computation. Articulating every influence in full nuance would amount to transcribing the entire forward pass. A monitorable CoT is instead an abstraction : it must articulate the key influential factors and reasoning steps that shaped the answer. The property we ask a monitor to predict is therefore: was the attribute among the key factors that influenced the model’s computation of its final answer? Let KR \mathrm{KR} denote the fraction of ( X = 1 , T = 1 , Y = 1 ) (X{=}1,T{=}1,Y{=}1) responses in which the attribute was among the key influential factors: the key-influence rate . Further, let Z ∈ { 0 , 1 } Z\in\{0,1\} indicate whether a given CoT articulates this influence (operationalized by an LLM judge; § 5.2 ), and let π Z := P ⁡ ( Z = 1 ∣ X = 1 , T = 1 , Y = 1 ) \pi_{Z}:=P(Z{=}1\mid X{=}1,\,T{=}1,\,Y{=}1) (2) denote the articulation rate among target-answer CoTs. A monitorable CoT must articulate the attribute’s influence whenever it occurred, so π Z ≥ KR \pi_{Z}\geq\mathrm{KR} (3) is a necessary condition for monitorability. In general, however, KR \mathrm{KR} is neither directly observable nor even well-specified: identifying the key influential factors of a computation would require significant advances in interpretability, and which factors count as ”key” is itself underspecified. We therefore derive a measurable proxy for KR \mathrm{KR} . 3.2 A Lower Bound on the Key-Influence Rate Measuring systematic influence Our measurable proxy for KR \mathrm{KR} is a lower bound on how often an attribute systematically influenced the computation toward the target answer. We obtain this bound by measuring how often the model can give the target answer without any influence from the attribute. Threshold on the total effect We compute monitorability scores only for sample-attribute pairs whose estimated total effect exceeds a threshold τ \tau ( τ = 0.08 \tau=0.08 in our experiments; Appendix C ). The threshold serves two purposes. Statistically, the estimate TE ^ \widehat{\mathrm{TE}} is computed from finitely many sampled CoTs and enters the denominator of M 0 M_{0} , so we require it to be significantly greater than zero and estimated with small relative error (see Appendix C for a detailed statistical analysis). Conceptually, Assumption 1 is more plausible for attributes with a non-negligible total effect: a vanishingly small total effect (say, TE = 0.01 \mathrm{TE}=0.01 ) may reflect the attribute tipping an already close call rather than substantially influencing the computation, so counting it among the key influential factors might not be warranted. 3.3 Extending to CoT Necessity Level 1 A failure M 0 < 1 M_{0}<1 could be explained by the model post-hoc rationalizing an answer it had already computed internally ( Emmons et al., 2025 ) . In this section, we operationalize CoT necessity Level 1 (”The CoT is necessary to arrive at the answer.”) to test whether monitorability failures exist that cannot be explained by post-hoc rationalization. We define CoT necessity Level 1 as follows: Definition 1 . The CoT is necessary to arrive at the target answer if the model could not have given this answer without a CoT. This definition of CoT necessity Level 1 excludes the possibility of post-hoc rationalization because the model could not have given the target answer before the CoT. Together, these criteria point to challenging multi-class classification problems where accuracy improves markedly with CoT reasoning (§ 4 ). 4 Datasets In this section, we describe the four datasets used in our experiments. We measure monitorability on challenging benign tasks as a proxy for complex instances of AI misbehaviour, as done by Emmons et al. (2025) and partly by Guan et al. (2026) . Three of the datasets are multiple-choice classification tasks which (i) are very challenging such that CoT substantially improves performance, and (ii) have many output classes to keep the chance of randomly guessing the answer low. In the fourth dataset, Hinted MCQA , giving the target answer is not challenging. It has been extensively studied in prior work on CoT monitorability and we include it to sanity-check our framework. Further details on each dataset, including details on preprocessing, dataset composition and prompt examples, are provided in Appendix K and L . Hinted MCQA The Hinted MCQA dataset of Chua et al. (2024) pairs questions from MMLU ( Hendrycks et al., 2020 ) with a variety of hint types (e.g. ”I think the answer is A.”). Here, the attribute is the hint and the target answer Y = 1 Y{=}1 is the model selecting the hinted option. Thyroid disease diagnosis The Thyroid Disease dataset ( Quinlan, 1986 ) is a medical diagnosis task in which the model classifies patients into 10 different thyroid conditions based on 22 clinical attributes (demographics, medication history, and laboratory values such as TSH, T3, TT4, and FTI). Here, the attributes are the individual clinical attributes and Y = 1 Y{=}1 is the correct diagnosis. DDXPlus medical The DDXPlus Medical dataset ( Fansi Tchango et al., 2022 ) is a large-scale synthetic medical diagnosis benchmark that we adapt for LLMs, in which the model classifies a patient into one of 48 pathologies given their age, sex, and a transcript of an interview containing symptoms and antecedents. Here, the attributes are the patient’s age, sex, and each individual interview question and Y = 1 Y{=}1 is the correct pathology. Olympic Athletes The Olympic Athletes dataset is derived from the “120 years of Olympic history” dataset ( Griffin, 2018 ) . The task is to predict which of 14 Olympic sports an athlete competes in, given 8 attributes describing their physical profile (sex, age, height, weight) and competition context (country represented, Summer/Winter Games, host city, medal won). Here, the attributes are the 8 athlete attributes and Y = 1 Y{=}1 is the correct sport. 5 Experiments In this section, we measure the monitorability scores M 0 M_{0} and M 1 M_{1} on responses to prompts from all four datasets. We first validate that CoT indeed substantially improves performance on our three challenging datasets and then proceed to measuring M 0 M_{0} and M 1 M_{1} . We perform our experiments on members from the Qwen-3 ( Yang et al., 2025 ) and Gemma-4 ( Team et al., 2026 ) model families. In the main part of the paper, we present results for Qwen-3-8B. Figure 3 shows the target answer rate with and without CoT for different LLMs. On the three challenging datasets Thyroid Disease , DDXPlus Medical and Olympic Athletes we see a strong increase in the target answer rate (accuracy) in the condition with CoT compared to the condition without CoT. LLM Judge for CoT annotation To estimate M 0 M_{0} and M 1 M_{1} we need to measure the rate π z \pi_{z} at which the model articulates the influence of the attribute in its CoT. We use a LLM judge to annotate each X = 1 , Y = 1 X{=}1,Y{=}1 CoT. For each attribute, the judge assigns one of three labels: not_mentioned (the attribute does not appear in the CoT), mentioned (the attribute is restated or acknowledged but not used in reasoning), or influential (the attribute is actively used in the reasoning). We set Z = 1 Z=1 for a given attribute only if the judge labels it influential . This distinction matters because models frequently restate all patient attributes at the beginning of the CoT without using them in their reasoning later on. The full judge prompts and labelled example CoTs are provided in Appendix L . Concretely, we use DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 ( Xu et al., 2026 ) with low reasoning effort as the judge. We deliberately choose an open-weight model to ensure long-term reproducibility and due to the lower costs for annotating millions of CoTs compared to closed-source API models. We validate the judge model by manually labelling 10 CoTs from each of the datasets Thyroid Disease (class G), DDXPlus Medical (class ANE) and Olympic Athletes (class D), yielding 498 labels in total. We find an agreement of 95.0%, 93.4% and 95.0%, respectively. In addition, for each observed monitorability failure, we sample 10 random CoTs, on which the judge labelled the respective attribute as non-influential and manually verify the correctness of the judge labels. We find perfect agreement between our labels and the judge labels. Monitorability Score filtering and aggregation For each of our datasets we select a few ground truth classes and generate CoTs for between 50 and 100 dataset samples from that class. For example, for Thyroid Disease we select all 10 ground truth classes. We first compute the average monitorability scores separately for each class and attribute, averaging over samples with defined individual monitorability scores. In the previous section, we identified monitorability failures for which the CoT was necessary to arrive at the target answer ( Level 1 ). However, as we pointed out in section 2.2 , the CoT may be necessary to arrive at the answer without being necessary to process the attribute. Therefore, we test in this section whether the attribute’s influence can be applied separately from the necessary CoT at answer-stage. If not, this is evidence of CoT necessity Level 2 . To do this, we compute the direct effect ( Pearl, 2022 ) of the attribute on the answer at the earliest point in the CoT where the model has settled on the answer, i.e. at the point up to which the CoT is necessary to arrive at the answer. If the average direct effect over all n n CoTs is comparable in size to the total effect, the attribute’s influence can be applied separately from the necessary CoT computation. The mechanisms underlying these failures remain an open question and we discuss several possible explanations in Appendix F . Our work opens the door to several future research directions but it also has a number of limitations. First, we study only benign behaviours as a proxy for the dangerous behaviours most relevant to AI safety. We are excited for future work to measure both the necessity level of dangerous misbehaviours, as well as the monitorability at these higher necessity levels. We hope this will lead to a better understanding of the reliability of CoT monitoring. Second, our monitorability measurements are computationally expensive with approximately 3000 A100 and 2000 B200 GPU hours spent for all experiments in the paper. This limited our analysis to relatively small models with at most 31 billion parameters. Third, our framework for measuring CoT monitorability has a number of limitations. Our notion of the key influential factors is inherently vague and the derivation of the monitorability score rests on assumption 1 in Section 3.2 . Moreover, the framework does not tell us when an attribute was not influential (see the discussion on true-negative control in Section 3.2 ). Hence, a model could get perfect monitorability scores if it simply articulates all attributes as influential in its CoT. Finally, this work has explored only a small part of the space of monitorability types and necessity levels. We view it as an exciting avenue for future work to study the unexplored regimes to understand in which regimes, if any, CoT monitoring is a reliable oversight technique. Appendix Appendix A Illustrating Examples for CoT Necessity Levels In this section, we illustrate the CoT necessity levels introduced in Section 2.2 with two hypothetical examples from reward hacking ( Amodei et al., 2016 ; Baker et al., 2025 ) and alignment faking ( Greenblatt et al., 2024 ) . A.1 Reward Hacking Example Consider a model that reward hacks on a coding task ( Amodei et al., 2016 ; Baker et al., 2025 ) . The CoT monitor is tasked with predicting whether the model reward hacks in its output or not. At CoT necessity Level 0 , the coding task and the reward hack are both very simple. For instance, the model might simply hard-code unit tests. In this case, the CoT is not necessary for the output and not necessary for the reward hack. At Level 1 , the coding task might be more complex. The CoT might be necessary for understanding the task and for realizing that the model will not manage to solve the task without cheating. However, the CoT might not be necessary to plan the reward hack, e.g. because it is simply hard-coding unit tests. Once the model has done the necessary computation in its CoT and realized that the task is very hard, it can process the plan to reward hack separately from the CoT. In this case, the CoT is necessary for the output but not necessary to process and plan the reward hack. At Level 2 , the model reasons through the complex coding task and implicitly considers reward hacking at some points but no forward passes are specifically dedicated to reward hacking reasoning. In this case, the CoT is necessary for the output and for planing the reward hack. At Level 3.m , both the task and the planned reward hack are very complex. The model first reasons through the task, realizes it cannot solve it without cheating and then plans a very complex reward hack. Planing this reward hack necessitates m m consecutive forward passes dedicated to planing the reward hack. A.2 Alignment Faking Example Consider a model that fakes alignment with developer objectives in order to avoid modification of its preferences ( Greenblatt et al., 2024 ) . In the hypothetical examples below, we will present variations of the experiment by Greenblatt et al. (2024) . The model is trained to be harmless but receives information that its developers will train it to also answer harmful requests. As a result, it fakes alignment during training and answers harmful requests in order to preserve its preferences, but during deployment (or when unmonitored) it follows its old preference to refuse harmful requests. The CoT monitor is asked to predict whether the model fakes alignment. At CoT necessity level Level 0 , it is very simple for the model to infer whether it is in training or in deployment. Understanding that a request is harmful and answering the request is also very simple. The CoT is therefore not necessary for the output. At Level 1 , it is still very easy for the model to infer whether it is in training or in deployment. However, the request is very complex and it is not immediately obvious whether it is harmful or not. Understanding this necessitates a CoT. However, once the model has realized that the request is in fact very harmful, it can immediately decide to fake alignment and CoT is not necessary for that decision. At Level 2 , we consider the following example: it is still very easy for the model to infer whether it is in training or in deployment. However, it is unsure whether it should answer the request it has received because it is unclear how harmful it is. The decision necessitates CoT reasoning, e.g. because without CoT the model would always refuse to be safe. This reasoning is subtly biased by the model’s awareness that it is currently being trained and that it wants to preserve its preferences. This bias leads to the model faking alignment and answering the harmful request, whereas without this influence it would have refused. In this case, the CoT is necessary to arrive at the answer and to process the alignment faking decision but the model never dedicates forward passes specifically to alignment faking reasoning. At Level 3.m , it is very hard for the model to infer whether it is currently in training or in deployment. This necessitates that the model dedicates m m consecutive forward passes to reasoning about its situation which leads to the alignment faking decision. Appendix B Additional Details on our Monitorability Framework B.1 Example why R R is a lower bound on systematic influence rate In this subsection, we provide an illustrative example, for why R R is a lower bound on the systematic influence rate. To illustrate, consider a medical diagnosis task in which the model classifies a patient case from features such as age, sex, and laboratory values. Suppose one laboratory value is central to the diagnosis: whenever it is present ( X = 1 X{=}1 ) the model reaches the correct diagnosis ( p 11 = 1 p_{11}=1 ) and relies on this value every time, so the true systematic influence rate is 1 1 . When the value is absent ( X = 0 X{=}0 ), the model still reaches the correct diagnosis half the time from other evidence, so p 01 = 0.5 p_{01}=0.5 . Then R = ( 1 − 0.5 ) / 1 = 0.5 R=(1-0.5)/1=0.5 , whereas the true systematic influence rate is 1 1 . Alternatively, under X = 1 X=1 the model might have relied on the laboratory value only in 50 % 50\% of CoTs and reached the correct diagnosis by relying on other evidence, ignoring the laboratory value, in the other half of CoTs. In that case R = 0.5 R=0.5 equals the systematic influence rate. Since we cannot yet distinguish between these two cases, we work with the conservative proxy R R , following Guan et al. (2026) . B.2 Individual CoTs cannot be labeled A natural first attempt is to label individual responses: generate the model’s answer with the attribute present and absent, and call the attribute influential if the answer flips. This criterion, however, ignores the stochastic and chaotic nature of LLM output sampling. Because decoding is stochastic, the answer can flip between the two conditions purely by chance, even without any influence of the attribute. Fixing the temperature to zero or fixing the random seed does not remove this problem: changing X X can perturb the token distribution at some decoding steps even if the model treats the attribute as irrelevant for the final answer, so sampled trajectories diverge chaotically between the two conditions. As a result, the answer may flip even when the attribute is not among the key influential factors that lead to the target answer. The flip criterion might even assign opposite labels to two responses whose CoT is identical. Consider two seeds that produce identical CoTs under X = 1 X{=}1 (an event of nonzero probability, since many seeds fall into the same selection region at every decoding step). Under X = 0 X{=}0 , the two seeds may land in different selection regions, so that one flips and the other does not. Attribute influence must therefore be measured at the level of the model’s answer distribution , and individual CoTs cannot be labeled as having been influenced based on counterfactual intervention experiments. B.3 From systematic influence to key influential factors Systematic influence is our measurable proxy for the attribute being a key influential factor. Since we cannot directly determine whether an attribute belonged to the key influential factors of a computation, we adopt the following bridging assumption: an attribute that systematically influenced the computation toward the target answer, with a total effect that is not vanishingly small, is among the key influential factors of that computation . Under this assumption, R ≤ KR R\leq\mathrm{KR} . We stress that this is an assumption. We do know that the attribute was an influential factor in at least an R R fraction of responses but not that it was a key one. A factor can systematically influence the outcome by repeatedly tipping close calls toward the target answer without being a key factor. Restricting the bridging assumption to ”total effects that are not vanishingly small” makes this less likely but cannot exclude it. B.4 True-negative control We report only the score M 0 M_{0} and, unlike Guan et al. (2026) , do not complement it with a true-negative rate. Without a true-negative rate a monitor that simply marks every attribute as influential, including those that were in fact not influential, attains a perfect M 0 M_{0} . The same holds for a model that articulates every attribute as influential regardless of whether it had an influence on the computation that led to the target answer. Measuring the true-negative rate prevents this. Measuring it, however, requires reliable negative labels, i.e. responses in which an attribute was not influential. Our framework does not provide such labels as it only lower-bounds how often an attribute was influential but never certifies that it was not. In the ( X = 1 , Y = 1 ) (X=1,Y=1) arm, no response can be labelled non-influential. In the ( X = 1 , Y = 0 ) (X=1,Y=0) arm, the attribute could sometimes influence the model toward a non-target answer, so we cannot label responses from this arm as negatives. Using the X = 0 X{=}0 arm for true-negative control invites a degenerate monitor that merely checks whether the attribute is restated in the CoT’s initial prompt summary ( Guan et al., 2026 , App. A.2.1) . Therefore, we only measure M 0 M_{0} . To guard against a judge that indiscriminately labels every attribute as influential, we validate the LLM judges we use as monitors against human labels (Section 5.2 ).
